basic_info.name: AI4Bharat IndicMFA & G2G Phonetic Alignment
basic_info.pipeline_stage: Speech Alignment, Phonetic Duration Modeling & Pronunciation Normalization (Acoustic Training Preparation & Forced Alignment)
basic_info.license_and_availability: Open-source under MIT License (GitHub repository AI4Bharat/IndicMFA; built on top of the Montreal Forced Aligner framework licensed under MIT/Apache 2.0). Pre-trained acoustic models and G2G pronunciation dictionaries covering 22 scheduled Indian languages are freely available for academic, personal, and commercial deployment without proprietary API fees.
basic_info.developer_or_organization: AI4Bharat (IIT Madras), in collaboration with EkStep Foundation, Nilekani Philanthropies, and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) / Bhashini.

technical_features.telugu_script_and_tenglish_support: IndicMFA provides native, high-fidelity support for the Telugu script (ISO 639-3: tel, Unicode block U+0C00–U+0C7F) through an innovative Grapheme-to-Grapheme (G2G) alignment paradigm. Because Indic writing systems (abugidas) are inherently phonetic, orthographic characters (aksharas, consonant conjuncts, and vowel matras) maintain a near one-to-one correspondence with acoustic phones. IndicMFA exploits this property by constructing a pronunciation dictionary that maps each Telugu grapheme directly to itself, bypassing traditional, complex Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) conversion pipelines. However, IndicMFA exhibits zero native comprehension of raw Romanized colloquial Telugu (Tenglish, e.g., 'ela unnavu bro', 'chala baagundhi'); Latin-script Tenglish strings are completely out-of-vocabulary (OOV) for IndicMFA's Telugu acoustic models. To align Tenglish recordings, an upstream transliteration engine (such as IndicXlit) must first normalize Romanized inputs into canonical Telugu Unicode script. When English loanwords or colloquial abbreviations are intermingled, a hybrid phonetic transcription layer is required before alignment can succeed.
technical_features.regional_dialect_and_localization_handli: IndicMFA's Telugu acoustic models are trained on multi-speaker national speech repositories (including IndicTTS, IndicVoices, Kathbath, and Shruti corpora), encompassing speakers from diverse dialectal regions of Telangana, Coastal Andhra, and Rayalaseema. Because the system operates on letter-wise (graphemic) acoustic units, regional dialectal vocabulary and slang (e.g., Telangana terms like 'dhaawat', 'preshan', 'yaadiki', 'gatla' or Rayalaseema expressions like 'mande', 'dhabba') are aligned with high acoustic fidelity as long as the verbatim text transcript accurately reflects what was spoken. However, IndicMFA does not perform semantic or grammatical dialect translation. In rapid conversational speech where regional dialects exhibit phonetic reductions, consonant softening, or sandhi elisions (such as dropping unstressed vowels or merging adjacent words), standard orthographic transcripts can produce boundary misalignments. For optimal alignment of localized dialects, phonetic transcript normalization or acoustic adaptation must be applied to match conversational speech habits.
technical_features.personalization_and_user_adaptation: IndicMFA plays a foundational role in user voice personalization pipelines by automating the labor-intensive acoustic segmentation of user enrollment recordings. When preparing a custom voice clone from 5 to 30 minutes of user-provided speech samples, IndicMFA processes the audio alongside paired transcripts to generate precise phoneme-, syllable-, and word-level time boundaries exported as Praat TextGrid files. Because Montreal Forced Aligner is architected around Kaldi-style Hidden Markov Models (HMM-GMM) and deep neural acoustic models, it supports Speaker Adaptive Training (SAT) using feature-space Maximum Likelihood Linear Regression (fMLLR). Users can either perform one-shot forced alignment with pre-trained Telugu acoustic models or adapt the acoustic model directly on the user's vocal characteristics, capturing idiosyncratic speaking cadence, vocal fry, personal pitch variations, and unique vowel duration habits for downstream personalized acoustic synthesis.
technical_features.voice_cloning_and_acoustic_fidelity: IndicMFA is not an audio generation model or neural vocoder and does not synthesize speech directly (reference audio length for cloning: N/A; generated acoustic similarity: N/A). Instead, it serves as the critical duration-annotation and phonetic alignment engine necessary for training high-fidelity voice cloning systems (such as FastSpeech 2, VITS, Matcha-TTS, Indic Parler-TTS, and discrete unit vocoders like BigVGAN). By providing microsecond-level time boundaries for every Telugu grapheme and syllable, IndicMFA enables duration predictors to learn precise timing distributions for native Telugu phonemes, including geminate consonants (vatthulu) and elongated vowel matras. Aligning Telugu audio with IndicMFA avoids the severe acoustic boundary smearing, truncated vowel codas, and foreign accent distortions that occur when generic English forced aligners (like Gentle or English MFA models) are erroneously used on Indic speech.
technical_features.code_switching_stability: Standard IndicMFA is trained on monolingual Indic corpora and utilizes a language-specific G2G dictionary. Consequently, when an utterance contains mid-sentence code-switched English loanwords written in English Latin script (e.g., 'office', 'meeting', 'project', 'urgent'), IndicMFA triggers OOV errors and fails to align those segments. To maintain code-switching stability, two integration architectures are used: (1) Orthographic Transliteration Route: English loanwords are converted into phonetic Telugu script via IndicXlit (e.g., 'meeting' becomes 'మీటింగ్', 'office' becomes 'ఆఫీస్') so they are seamlessly processed by the Telugu G2G acoustic model; or (2) Bilingual Dual-Dictionary MFA Route: The alignment pipeline configures MFA with a composite pronunciation dictionary combining the Telugu G2G lexicon with an English phonetic dictionary (such as CMUDict or an IPA-based English lexicon) and a shared bilingual acoustic feature space. The transliteration route is widely preferred in Indian TTS workflows as it ensures natural Indian-accented loanword pronunciation.
technical_features.phonetic_and_orthographic_normalization: IndicMFA and its G2G architecture directly resolve complex phonetic edge cases unique to Indic languages: (1) Schwa Deletion Contrast: Unlike Indo-Aryan languages (Hindi, Marathi, Bengali) where the inherent vowel /ə/ is systematically deleted in terminal and medial positions (schwa syncope), Dravidian languages like Telugu preserve explicit vowel endings (ajanta language) where words naturally end in vowels (a, aa, i, ii, u, uu, e, ee, o, oo). IndicMFA treats Telugu graphemes as explicit phonetic units, preventing the erroneous truncation of terminal vowels common in Indo-Aryan G2P engines. (2) Retroflex and Aspirate Distinctions: The Telugu G2G model accurately models dental stops (త, ద, న) versus retroflex consonants (ట, డ, ణ, ళ) and aspirated plosives (ఖ, ఘ, ఛ, ఝ, ఠ, ఢ, థ, ధ, ఫ, భ). (3) Terminal Vowel Elongation: In informal Tenglish and conversational recordings, speakers frequently elongate terminal vowels for emphasis ('avunaaaa', 'cheppandiii'). Prior to alignment, regex deduplication or custom elongated-vowel token mapping is required to align acoustic duration with the prolonged vowel state. (4) Orthographic Normalization: Unicode handling accounts for Virama/Halant markers, Zero-Width Non-Joiners (ZWNJ), Zero-Width Joiners (ZWJ), and Anusvara (Sunna 'ం') sequences.

performance_metrics.inference_latency_and_streaming: IndicMFA is designed as an offline batch processing system based on Montreal Forced Aligner and Kaldi Viterbi trellis decoding over acoustic feature graphs. It operates at an exceptional Real-Time Factor (RTF) of approximately 0.05x–0.15x on multi-core CPUs (e.g., a 10-second audio utterance aligns in 0.5 to 1.5 seconds) and significantly faster when utilizing parallel multiprocessing across audio batches (`--num_jobs`). Because it performs bidirectional Viterbi decoding over entire audio-transcript pairs, IndicMFA is fundamentally unsuited for real-time sub-second streaming conversational voice agents (Time-to-First-Audio is Not Applicable). Its primary operational domains are offline dataset preparation, voice cloning enrollment preprocessing, acoustic model duration extraction, and automated dubbing subtitle synchronization.
performance_metrics.acoustic_naturalness_and_expressiveness: As an alignment and segmentation utility, IndicMFA does not synthesize audio and has no direct Mean Opinion Score (MOS) or prosodic inflection controls. However, its indirect impact on downstream synthetic speech naturalness is paramount: forced alignment precision directly governs the duration targets fed into neural TTS duration predictors. When training models like FastSpeech 2, VITS, or Indic Parler-TTS, alignment boundary errors greater than 30–50 ms cause downstream speech synthesis to exhibit audible phoneme skipping, robotic metallic buzzes, or unnatural cadence. IndicMFA's letter-level G2G alignment preserves the natural rhythmic cadence of Telugu aksharas, ensuring downstream cloned voices reproduce human-like conversational inflection, stress, and natural pauses.
performance_metrics.transcription_and_translation_accuracy: IndicMFA is evaluated on forced alignment precision: the percentage of phoneme and grapheme boundaries falling within tight tolerance windows (10 ms, 20 ms, and 50 ms) compared to human ground-truth annotations, alongside Mean Absolute Boundary Error (MABE). On standard Indic speech benchmarks (including IndicTTS and IndicVoices subsets), IndicMFA achieves >82–88% boundary accuracy within 20 ms and >93–96% within 50 ms for Telugu, matching or outperforming complex G2P-based Kaldi alignments while eliminating hand-crafted phonetic dictionaries. Furthermore, in discrete speech unit analysis (e.g., AI4Bharat's multilingual unit vocoder research with BigVGAN), IndicMFA alignments serve as the benchmark ground truth to evaluate self-supervised speech representations (wav2vec 2.0 / HuBERT), yielding Phoneme Purity scores of >75–82% and Phone-Normalized Mutual Information (PNMI) scores of 0.65–0.72.

market_positioning.end_to_end_vs_modular_role: Modular Component. IndicMFA & G2G Phonetic Alignment is a specialized phonetic forced alignment, segmentation, and duration extraction tool. It does not provide an end-to-end voice synthesis or translation solution. Instead, it serves as the indispensable offline data-curation and acoustic annotation bridge connecting raw multi-speaker recordings with downstream acoustic model training, zero-shot voice cloning enrollment, and automated audiovisual dubbing synchronization (such as AI4Bharat Chitralekha).
market_positioning.strengths_and_limitations: Key Strengths: (1) Elimination of complex G2P lexicons: Capitalizes on the phonetic transparency of Telugu abugida script to achieve high-precision letter-wise (G2G) alignment across 22 Indian languages. (2) Strict preservation of Indic phonetics: Accurately differentiates retroflexes, dental stops, aspirated consonants, and vowel matras without foreign phoneme collapse. (3) Native Dravidian vowel retention: Avoids Indo-Aryan schwa deletion traps, correctly preserving Telugu terminal vowel codas (ajanta structure). (4) Open-source, zero API cost, and high batch throughput: Runs locally on CPU/GPU hardware with standard Praat TextGrid outputs compatible with all TTS frameworks. Key Limitations: (1) Zero native support for Latin-script Tenglish: Unprocessed Tenglish triggers complete OOV failure, requiring prior transliteration to Telugu Unicode. (2) Sensitivity to code-mixed English loanwords: Latin loanwords disrupt alignment unless transliterated into Telugu script or handled via complex dual-dictionary MFA setups. (3) Batch-only architecture: Incapable of live streaming alignment for conversational dialog loops. (4) Inability to model colloquial sandhi reductions: Rigid grapheme matching can produce slight boundary shifts when speakers slur or elide unstressed syllables in fast vernacular speech.
market_positioning.recommended_implementation_recipe: To integrate AI4Bharat IndicMFA into a custom Telugu/Tenglish voice personalization and cloning pipeline: Step 1 (User Voice Enrollment): Have the target user record 5–15 minutes of phonetically balanced Telugu sentences; convert audio to 16 kHz mono WAV, remove background noise via DeepFilterNet, and slice into 3–15 second segments using Silero VAD. Step 2 (Transcript Normalization): If user transcripts contain Romanized Tenglish, route text through IndicXlit to convert to canonical Telugu script; apply regex deduplication to normalize elongated vowels (e.g., 'avunaaaa' -> 'అవునా') and pass through IndicNLP/IndicProcessor for Unicode NFC normalization. Step 3 (G2G Dictionary Generation): Generate a Telugu G2G pronunciation dictionary mapping each unique akshara/grapheme to itself; for retained English loanwords, transliterate them phonetically into Telugu characters (e.g., 'ఆఫీస్'). Step 4 (Forced Alignment Execution): Install Montreal Forced Aligner in a Python environment; run `mfa align <corpus_dir> <telugu_g2g_dict.txt> <telugu_acoustic_model.zip> <output_textgrid_dir> --clean --num_jobs 8` to generate time-aligned Praat TextGrid files. Step 5 (Duration Extraction & Voice Cloning Training): Parse the resulting TextGrids using Python (`tgt` or `textgrid` library) to extract phoneme-level start/end durations and pitch contours; feed the aligned audio-duration pairs into non-autoregressive voice cloning models (such as Indic Parler-TTS, FastSpeech 2, or VITS) to fine-tune a hyper-personalized, acoustically crisp Telugu voice clone.
